clue.text: Hardly any at low tide?

blocks.note: surface reading: the sea has scarcely any water in it when the tide is out
setter's reading: an amount so tiny it is lost in the sea, an idiom for something negligible

explanation.surface: Someone peers at a beach at low water and finds almost nothing left in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the tide is a red herring: the phrase is the idiom for a negligible quantity, which happens to mention the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a contribution so small compared with the whole that it makes no real difference.

clue.text: Note correct working place in 19 once

blocks.note: B is a musical note
correct means right
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A notice correcting the record about a workplace in a county as it used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 refers to the answer at 19-across, East Sussex. Brighton, the seaside city, was in that county until it became a separate unitary authority, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The south-coast resort city lay within that county's boundaries before local government reorganisation separated it.

clue.text: Teabags in cups, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: the country whose tea fills them
second meaning: porcelain crockery, of which cups are an example

explanation.surface: Someone brewing tea by dropping the bags straight into the cups.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one image of making tea; the two halves are separate meanings of one word, the tea-producing country and fine crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: China tea is a classic blend sold in bags, and porcelain tableware such as cups is called china.

clue.text: Fashion belt with care — it's an accessory

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the following letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to style a belt carefully, since it is a fashion accessory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like part of the clothing picture, but it is the verb telling you to rearrange the two words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracelet is jewellery worn on the wrist, a typical example of a fashion accessory.

clue.text: Stay with me up in shower

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top, backwards
one word placed in another is put inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
a shower is a spell of rain

explanation.surface: An invitation to linger together in the shower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' suggests a bathroom, but it is the weather sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay and to remain are verbal synonyms, both meaning to continue in the same place.

clue.text: Plot many intended to listen to

indicators.note: something meant to be listened to is heard, so the sound of the words counts, not their spelling

blocks.note: many is a lot, and intended is meant

explanation.surface: A storyline that many people were supposed to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' reads as a storyline, but it is a piece of land. An allotment is a small rented plot of land for growing vegetables, common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is a small parcel of ground rented for gardening, so it is a plot in the land sense.

clue.text: Procure job with no top on — initially, that's all it needs

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so it is taken off
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each word is used

blocks.note: taken as written before beheading
the first letters of the four words that's, all, it and needs

explanation.surface: Advice that landing a job takes only going topless, a cheeky line about getting hired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it needs' reads as a link phrase but its words supply letters too: 'initially' covers the whole run of four words.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure and to obtain both mean to get hold of something, often with some effort.

clue.text: Chaotic finished article on location

blocks.note: something finished is all over
the definite article
a location is a place

explanation.surface: A wrecked item turns up at some site.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' means one piece sits on top of the next.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for something disorganised or scattered everywhere, which is what chaotic describes.

clue.text: Black Beauty, an unexpected winner?

blocks.note: first meaning, literally: Black Beauty is the black horse of Anna Sewell's novel
second meaning: a little-known contender who surprises everyone by succeeding

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the famous fictional horse could win a race against the odds.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Beauty, the horse in the classic children's novel, is literally a horse of dark colour; the idiom means a surprise success.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an outsider whose abilities were unknown until they won, drawn from horse racing.

clue.text: Ultimately, vitriol and bile stirred up calumny

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept
stirring something up mixes it, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the last letter of vitriol
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Venom and bitterness whipped up into a slanderous attack.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one image of spite; the vitriol and bile are just letter sources.
explanation.definitionFit: Calumny is a false statement damaging someone's reputation, and libel is the written form of exactly that.

clue.text: Fifteen in charge is natural

blocks.note: refers to the answer at 15-down, a newspaper, which can be called an organ
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A rugby team of fifteen being led in an unforced way.
explanation.walkthrough: Fifteen looks like a rugby side, but it points to the answer at 15-down; an organ is a newspaper or journal that speaks for a group.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic produce is grown without artificial chemicals, so organic serves as a synonym for natural.

clue.text: Green party following not quite as vocal

indicators.note: something not quite complete stops short, so each word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut short
taken as written, then cut short
a do is a party

explanation.surface: An environmental party trailing in the polls, not as outspoken as its rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green party' looks like the political party, but the clue splits there: Green is the definition. 'following' places the party word after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Avocado is the name of a dull yellowish-green colour, taken from the fruit's flesh.

clue.text: Tiny part of moon, thanks

blocks.note: Io is one of Jupiter's moons
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Gratitude for a small piece of the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota, from the smallest Greek letter, means the smallest possible amount or bit of something.

clue.text: Clean man-bag, removing a boiled sweet

indicators.note: removing means taking away, so the named letter is dropped from the fodder
boiling churns things up, so the remaining letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
the single letter to take out

explanation.surface: Instructions to wash a man's handbag, though leaving out a boiled sweet in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boiled sweet' reads as a hard candy, but the phrase splits: boiled is the anagram signal and sweet alone is the definition, a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A blancmange is a set milk pudding, and in British usage a pudding or dessert is called a sweet.

clue.text: Snapper we cooked daily

indicators.note: cooking transforms raw ingredients, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fish we prepare for dinner every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' looks like an adverb for how often the fish is cooked, but it is the noun: a paper published every day.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a newspaper that comes out every day, a common noun use of the adjective.

clue.text: Beat guy with line

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
a guy is a man, a gent

explanation.surface: Thrashing some fellow who has a rope or a line.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a tangent is a straight line touching a curve at one point.

clue.text: Wee dram for the infant

blocks.note: wee is Scottish for small, tiny
a dram is a small measure of spirits, a tot

explanation.surface: A small whisky poured out for a baby, a comically inappropriate drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee and dram suggest a Scottish whisky measure; the drink is just a word for a small person.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny tot is an affectionate phrase for a very young child or toddler.

clue.text: Stir to let tea dry

indicators.note: stirring mixes things around, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions to stir the brew and then leave it to dry out.
explanation.walkthrough: The tea fits the surface neatly, since teetotallers drink tea rather than alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry describes a person or place without alcohol, which is what teetotal means for someone who abstains.

clue.text: Wrong attempt to package an item of underwear

indicators.note: packaging wraps one thing around another, so one word encloses the next

blocks.note: an attempt is a try
taken as written
in British English a vest is a sleeveless undershirt

explanation.surface: A misguided bid to gift-wrap some underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a vest is worn under a shirt, not over it as in American English.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grossly unjust or absurd distortion, a wrong done to something, as in a travesty of justice.

clue.text: The Guardian chases criminal asset to the other county

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled
the clue appears in the Guardian, so the paper refers to itself as us
'the other' is a coy British euphemism for sex

explanation.surface: The newspaper pursues a stolen asset across the border into the next county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chases' means the paper's word comes after the jumbled asset. East Sussex is a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: East Sussex is one of the ceremonial counties of England, home to Brighton and Hastings.

clue.text: "Ice cream on day off", it's said

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so the sound of the word matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: Sunday is the traditional day off work

explanation.surface: A quoted rule that ice cream is only for days off.
explanation.definitionFit: A sundae is a dessert of ice cream topped with syrup, fruit or nuts.

clue.text: Soldier, coy on the outside, delivers a song

indicators.note: being on the outside means wrapping around something, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: coy means shy
a soldier ant is a caste of ant, so soldier stands for ANT

explanation.surface: A bashful soldier stands up and sings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier' looks like a military man, but in crosswords it is often the insect, after soldier ants.
explanation.definitionFit: A shanty is a rhythmic work song traditionally sung by sailors hauling ropes.

clue.text: Horseman changes side

indicators.note: the sides are left and right, so one side's letter is swapped for the other's

blocks.note: a man is a male

explanation.surface: A rider switches to the other flank of his mount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horseman' looks like one word, but it splits: Horse is the definition. L for left becomes R for right.
explanation.definitionFit: A mare is an adult female horse, so it is a kind of horse.

clue.text: Check the depth exactly

blocks.note: first meaning: to measure water depth with a weighted line
second meaning: precisely

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one instruction to measure carefully; the two parts are a verb and an adverb sharing one spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumb line measures soundings, and the adverb plumb means precisely or squarely, as in plumb centre.

clue.text: Music in wedding venue is rubbish

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: Cana is where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding
tat is cheap rubbish

explanation.surface: A complaint that the band at the wedding reception is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: The wedding venue is the biblical one: the wedding at Cana in John's Gospel.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a choral and orchestral composition, often sacred, so it is a piece of music.

clue.text: Boring source of energy?

blocks.note: surface reading: a dull, tedious kind of power supply
setter's reading: boring means drilling, so the source is something drilled into the ground

explanation.surface: A grumble about an uninspiring form of power generation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull, but it means drilling a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Petroleum is extracted through a drilled shaft, and crude from that shaft is a major fuel supply.

clue.text: Kinky magazines removing sign — shock!

indicators.note: removing means taking away, so those letters are struck out of the fodder
kinky means twisted, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to take out

explanation.surface: Someone is scandalised when risqué magazines turn up without their warning label.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of sign are scattered through the fodder rather than sitting together, which is fine because the remainder is jumbled anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: To amaze someone is to astonish them, close in sense to the verb shock.

clue.text: Disturbing and not quite mature to be larking about at ninety-nine

indicators.note: not quite complete means falling short by the last letter
larking about is fooling around, so the letters are played with and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut short and jumbled
taken as written
I before C is one less than a hundred in Roman numerals, a crossword shorthand

explanation.surface: Finding it upsetting that a 99-year-old still behaves immaturely.
explanation.walkthrough: IC for 99 is not strictly correct Roman (XCIX is), but setters use it freely.
explanation.definitionFit: Something traumatic causes deep emotional upset, so it is distressing or disturbing.
